q: In strength design, what does the "strength" of a member mean?
o: Its capacity to resist the factored loads
n: Strength is what the member can carry. The design check is φ × nominal strength ≥ the effect of the factored loads.

q: In seismic design, what is the lateral-force-resisting system?
o: The part of the structure designed to carry the design seismic forces
n: Not every member resists earthquakes. The lateral system (frames, braces, walls and diaphragms) is designed and detailed for the seismic forces; the rest must only follow the drift safely.

q: What is a cantilevered column system?
o: A column that projects from a wall
A row of columns braced by diagonals
A lateral system whose columns act as cantilevers fixed at the base, with little moment capacity at the top
A column carried by a transfer beam
n: Each column resists lateral load like a flagpole, fixed at its footing. Such systems get a low R value because they have little redundancy.

q: What defines a bearing wall system?
o: It has a complete frame for gravity loads
It uses cables for all loads
It has no complete vertical load-carrying space frame, so walls carry the gravity loads
n: In a bearing wall system the walls carry most gravity loads and also resist lateral forces. In a building frame system a complete frame carries gravity load and walls or braces take the lateral load.

q: In NSCP wind design, what is the design force F used for?
o: Wind loads on open buildings and other structures
n: For enclosed and partially enclosed buildings, wind is applied as a design pressure p. For open buildings and other structures (signs, towers, chimneys), an equivalent static force F is used.

q: A warehouse has a large open door on its windward wall and almost no other openings. How is it classified for wind design?
n: When windward openings exceed the rest of the openings by more than 10% (and pass the size test), wind rushes in and pressurizes the interior. Partially enclosed buildings have the highest internal pressure coefficient, ±0.55.

q: A ground floor has only 70% of the lateral strength of the floor above. Which irregularity is this?
n: Strength below 80% of the story above makes it a weak story. The same ratio for stiffness (below 70%) would make it a soft story.

q: In the figure, which system resists lateral load with a shear wall?
n: C is a solid wall that resists force in its own plane, like a deep vertical cantilever. Walls are very stiff and limit drift well, but they block openings.

q: How are the members of a concentrically braced frame mainly loaded?
n: In a concentric brace the member lines meet at points, so the frame works like a truss and the braces carry tension or compression. Eccentric braces are offset on purpose so a short link yields in shear.

q: What is a boundary element?
o: A reinforced zone along the edges of a shear wall, diaphragm or opening
n: The edges of a shear wall carry the highest compression and tension from overturning. Boundary elements, with extra bars and closely spaced ties, keep those edges from crushing or buckling.

q: In NSCP wind design, what is the design pressure p used for?
o: Wind loads on signs and towers only
Wind loads on enclosed and partially enclosed buildings
n: Design pressure is the equivalent static wind pressure on building surfaces, combining external and internal pressure coefficients.

q: For wind design, which buildings have the highest internal pressure?
o: All have the same internal pressure
n: A large windward opening lets wind pressurize the interior, which pushes out on the roof and leeward walls. NSCP uses GCpi = ±0.55 for partially enclosed buildings, ±0.18 for enclosed and 0 for open.

q: Why do wind enclosure classifications matter in design?
o: They set the internal pressure, which adds to the external pressure on walls and roof
They set the building's fire rating
n: The same wind gives very different net pressures depending on whether it can enter the building. Roof uplift on a partially enclosed building can be far higher than on an enclosed one.

q: An open parking ground floor has 60% of the lateral stiffness of the infilled floor above. Which irregularity is this?
n: Stiffness below 70% of the story above is a soft story. Earthquake drift concentrates there, and many collapses in past earthquakes started in soft ground floors.

q: What does a floor diaphragm do in a lateral-force system?
o: It carries only the gravity load to the beams
It resists uplift at the foundation
It carries the lateral forces at each level to the vertical resisting elements
It seals the building against water
n: The floor slab acts like a deep horizontal beam, collecting inertia forces and delivering them to the frames or walls. Large openings or re-entrant corners weaken it.

q: In the figure, which system is a braced frame?
n: B uses diagonal members, so the frame acts like a vertical truss. Braced frames are stiff and economical but the diagonals get in the way of openings.

q: For wind design, what makes a building "flexible"?
o: A fundamental natural frequency below 1 Hz
n: Buildings with a natural frequency under 1 Hz, often slender ones taller than four times their least width, can be set swaying by gusts, so a gust-effect factor for dynamic response is required.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what defines a low-rise building for wind design?
o: An enclosed or partially enclosed building with mean roof height of 18 m or less, not exceeding its least horizontal dimension
Any building with a flat roof
n: Low-rise buildings (h ≤ 18 m and h ≤ least horizontal dimension) may use simplified envelope procedures for wind loads.

q: How is an enclosed building defined for wind design?
o: As a building with no doors
As a building with all walls 80% open
As a building that does not meet the requirements for open or partially enclosed buildings
As a building with a flat roof
n: Enclosed is the default class: if neither the open test nor the partially enclosed test is met, the building is enclosed.

q: A 3.0 m high story drifts 45 mm relative to the floor below. What is its drift ratio?
n: Drift ratio = Δ / h = 45 / 3,000 = 0.015, which is under the NSCP limit of 0.025 for shorter buildings.

q: What is a horizontal bracing system?
o: A horizontal truss that acts as a diaphragm
A row of diagonal braces in a wall
A set of beams that carry gravity load only
n: Where a roof or floor cannot act as a diaphragm, such as a light metal roof, horizontal cross-bracing in the plane of the roof carries the lateral forces to the walls or frames.

q: In the figure, which system resists lateral load only through rigid beam-column joints?
n: A is a moment-resisting frame: without braces or walls, its beams and columns must bend to resist sway, so its joints must be rigid. It leaves the bays open for doors and windows.

q: What is base shear?
o: The shear in the roof beams
The total design lateral force at the base of the structure
The shear stress in a column
n: Static-force design finds the base shear first (V = CvIW/RT, within limits) and then distributes it up the height as floor forces.

q: For wind design, what are components and cladding?
o: The main frames and shear walls
Elements of the envelope that do not qualify as part of the main wind-force-resisting system
n: Components and cladding include roof sheets, purlins, wall panels, windows and their fasteners. They are designed for higher local pressures than the main system because they take gusts over small areas.

q: A covered court has walls on all four sides that are each 85% open. How is it classified for wind design?
n: A building is open when every wall is at least 80% open. Wind passes through, so internal pressure is taken as zero.
